Stiff-Three Limbs Syndrome
Video
Stiff-Person syndrome (SPS), is a rare and disabling disor-
der characterized by rigidity and painful episodic spasms that

involve axial and limb musculature with continuous, involun-
tary motor-unit activity (CMUA) at rest in electrophysiologi-
cal studies.
1 SPS can be subdivided into stiff-trunk syndrome,
stiff-limb syndrome (SLS), and progressive encephalomyelitis
with rigidity. 1 The cause of this disorder is unknown; how-
ever, an autoimmune pathogenesis is suspected. 1
We report a patient diagnosed with stiff-three limbs syn-
drome (STLS), without CMUA, successfully treated with in-
travenous immunoglobulin.
An 11-year-old girl was admitted to the Movement Disor-
ders Unit of the Hospital de Clı ´nicas of the Federal Univer-
sity of Parana´ (Brazil) with a 2-year history of limb ‘ ‘paraly-
sis’ ’ and dysarthria. Symptoms started 1 week after an upper
respiratory tract viral infection in the form of progressive,
ﬂuctuating, and painful rigidity in the right upper and both
lower limbs. Initially she complained of frequent falls and
later rigidity in the affected limbs became ﬁxed, with dis-
abling gait disturbance and associated with severe dysarthria
(video 1). Previous personal and family medical histories
were unremarkable.
Neurological examination showed severe dysarthria with
no other abnormalities in cranial nerves assessment. Lower
limbs and right upper limbs showed diffuse livedo reticularis
with skin coldness in comparison with the nonaffected left
upper limb. Limbs were normotrophic with moderate to
severe rigidity in the lower limbs and right upper limb, with
proportionate proximal and distal distribution. The left upper

limb showed no signs of abnormal tone strength, despite the
subjective complaint of paralysis. Deep tendon reﬂexes were
brisk, symmetric, and plantar reﬂexes were ﬂexor. Laboratory
tests included normal leukocytes, red cells, and platelet
counts; normal plasma glucose, creatinine, electrolytes, anti-
cardiolipin, antinuclear antibodies, TSH and CK levels; nor-
mal erythrocyte sedimentation rate; negative syphilis, hepati-
tis B/C, and HIV serologies; cerebral spinal ﬂuid analysis
was unremarkable as well as brain and spinal chord MRI and
electromyography with nerve conduction studies of the upper
and lower limbs and paraspinal muscles. Plasma autoantibod-
ies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD) were positive
(2.6 U/mL).
The symptoms remained unchanged during treatment with
baclofen (up to 40 mg/day, for 1 month) or diazepam (30
mg/day for 20 days). After 3 months, intravenous immuno-
globulin was started and repeated for 1 year (initial dose:
0.4 g/kg/day for ﬁve consecutive days, followed by monthly
doses of 0.4 g/kg administered for 1 day). During this pe-
riod, the patient showed signiﬁcant improvement of rigidity
and gait performance with mild improvement in dysarthria
(video 2: after 1 year of follow-up and video 3: after 3
years of follow-up).
The case reported here describ es a patient with a distinct
clinical presentation of SPS, namely painful stiffness in
three limbs and dysarthria, with no features such as sphinc-
ter disturbances, truncal rigid ity, exaggerated lumbar lordo-
sis, or CMUA.

We designated the case presented here as STLS (asymmet-
rical rigidity in three limbs, associated with dysarthria, with-
out continuous motor unit activity), successfully treated with
intravenous immunoglobulin.
Legends to the Video
Segment 1. Baseline evaluation showing the patient with
lower limbs and right upper limb rigidity, with proportionate
proximal and distal distribution.
Segment 2. After 1 year of treatment with intravenous im-
munoglobulin, the patient showed signiﬁcant improvement of
rigidity and gait performance.
Segment 3. After 3 years, the patient persists with signiﬁ-
cant symptom improvement.
